turns.content:
I found the court judgment yesterday, tucked in his mail stack. $12,400 defaulted. Wage garnishment imminent. I froze the joint lease, canceled the moving van, called him a fraud to his face.

• Was that an overreaction, or was I right to hit the brakes that hard.

You were right to hit the brakes. The word you used is the only part I’d put on a shorter leash.

A $12,400 **default** judgment with garnishment coming is not a “we’ll sort it after the boxes are in” surprise. Default usually means he got sued and didn’t deal with it. Garnishment means a court is about to take a slice of his paycheck before rent, groceries, or you. Freezing a **joint** lease and killing the van was you refusing to legally chain yourself to that. That’s not hysteria. That’s not signing a contract while the other person’s income is about to get a court-ordered first cut.

Calling him a fraud to his face is the heat. Hiding a live judgment while you two were about to share an address is a serious trust breach. It can be shame, freeze, chaos, or actual deceit — you don’t know which yet from a piece of mail. “Fraud” is a specific charge. “You let me almost move in without telling me the court is coming for your wages” is already enough.

So: the stop was proportionate. The label may have been. You don’t have to unsay the anger to be fair. You *do* need the actual story before you decide if this is a one-lie crisis or a pattern — what the debt is, whether there’s more, and why you found it in a stack instead of hearing it from him.

You protected the expensive part. You didn’t move in first and ask later.

• He offered to sleep in his car until it's sorted. Said the debt is his sister's unpaid medical bills.

I told him no. He can't stay in our sublet tonight.

• Was that too far.

Not on the move. On tonight, you’re closer to the line.

Freezing the joint lease was still the right call. A default judgment and garnishment don’t become cute because he says it’s his sister’s medical bills. If the court is coming for *his* wages, it’s his problem on paper, whatever the origin story is. You don’t have to believe that in the hallway at midnight.

Barring him from the sublet tonight is a different thing. You found a hidden money bomb, not a reason he is unsafe in the room. Needing space is fair. Making the only option a car, same night, is the part that starts to look like punishment instead of a boundary. “Until it’s sorted” is also a trap — that could be weeks.

A cleaner split:

- **The new lease / the van:** stay stopped. Don’t un-cancel anything on a speech.
- **Tonight:** if he has a friend, a hotel, family (including the sister this debt supposedly belongs to), he can use that. You don’t have to play host while you’re still shaking. You also don’t have to send him to a parking lot to prove you’re serious.
- **The story:** tomorrow, documents. Whose name is on the judgment, what court, what’s actually in default, whether there’s more. Sister’s bills can be real. They can also be the easiest sentence in the world.

You were right to hit the brakes on tying your housing to his paycheck. You don’t have to let him sleep in the car to keep that decision.

• He said he'll stay at his brother's tonight. Not the car. So that's handled for now.

But he also said the sister's bills are in his name because she had no credit. He co-signed years ago, then she stopped paying.

• Does that change anything.

It changes the *story*. It does not change the *risk*.

If he’s telling the truth, this is not “secret gambling / fake identity.” It’s the classic family trap: he co-signed because she had no credit, she stopped paying, the collector sued *him*, and a default judgment means he didn’t handle the lawsuit. Co-signing is not a favor that stays on her. On paper it is his debt. Garnishment still hits *his* paycheck. A joint lease still puts you next to an income that’s about to get a court-ordered cut.

What it does *not* fix:

- You found it in the mail, not from him, right before you were about to share housing.
- “Years ago” plus a default judgment usually means this did not sneak up last Tuesday. Summons, missed deadlines, then garnishment. That’s a long silence.
- Sister’s medical bills can be real. They are also the easiest, most sympathetic sentence in the world. You don’t have to decide tonight which one it is.

Brother tonight is the right landing. Keep the lease frozen. Don’t unsay the stop because the origin got sadder.

What would actually move the needle is paper, not the hallway version: whose name is on the judgment, which court, the date, whether he was served, what’s left after any sister payments, and whether this is the only one. Until that’s in front of you, treat it as *his* legal problem that he hid while you two were about to sign a joint lease — even if he did it for her.

• He wants me to sign just the lease today, says he'll fix the garnishment next week and I'll never see a deduction.

• That's a 5 PM deadline. What do I actually do.

Do not sign. Not at 5 PM. Not on a promise.

A same-day lease deadline is pressure, not a reason. “I’ll fix the garnishment next week and you’ll never see a deduction” does not protect you. Garnishment hits *his* paycheck. A **joint** lease hits *you* for the full rent if that paycheck comes up short. You will not see a line item called garnishment. You will see whether rent is paid. Default judgments also do not reliably vanish in a week. Vacating a default, settling $12,400, or stopping a wage order is paperwork, the other side, and a court — not a vibe.

**Today, before 5:**

- Do not go to the leasing office. Do not “just sign so we don’t lose it.”
- Tell him in writing, short: *I’m not signing a joint lease while there’s a default judgment and garnishment in play. That’s not changing today. Keep staying at your brother’s.*
- If the 5 PM is the landlord: *We’re not proceeding. I’m not signing.* You can lose the unit. That is cheaper than being on the hook for rent next to a $12k judgment.
- Do not argue the sister story in the hallway. Co-signed medical bills can be true and still be *his* debt on paper. It does not make a joint lease safe.

**What would actually have to happen before you even reopen this** — later, not tonight: the judgment in writing (court, case number, amount, date), whether a garnishment order has issued, a real plan (settlement, payment order, or vacated default), and his numbers after the cut. “You’ll never see it” is not that.

Brother tonight stays the plan. Lease stays frozen. Van stays canceled. You already did the hard stop; don’t undo it because the clock is loud.

• So sign nothing today and lose the unit. That's the clean move.

• But he's at his brother's with a trash bag of clothes, texting me receipts from 2019. And the clock is ticking.

• I'm not asking if I should sign. I'm asking if I'm being cruel or just careful.

You’re being careful. The trash bag is making it *feel* like cruelty. Those are not the same thing.

Losing the unit is you refusing a joint legal hook while a $12,400 default and garnishment are live. That’s not punishment. That’s not signing your name next to a paycheck a court is about to cut. The 5 PM clock is the landlord’s, or his panic. It is not a moral timer on you.

What’s happening on his end is real and sad: brother’s couch, a bag of clothes, 2019 receipts flying in. That can all be true — co-signed medical bills, sister with no credit, years of this sitting there — and it still doesn’t make a same-day joint lease safe. Receipts from 2019 are not a plan. They’re an origin story, sent under a deadline, after you found the judgment in the mail. Careful people don’t reverse a housing decision because the story got documented at 4 PM.

Cruel would be: sending him to a car when he had a brother, humiliating him for sport, treating him as disposable, or using the debt as a forever verdict. You already didn’t do the car. Brother tonight is handled. Not signing is the remaining line.

You can be decent without being available as a co-signer. Short, not theatrical: you’re not signing, the unit can go, he can stay at his brother’s, you’re not debating this by text until the judgment and garnishment are actually in front of you. Kindness is how you say it. Carefulness is what you don’t put your name on.

The guilt is the cost of not abandoning yourself. It doesn’t mean you chose wrong.
